core_hypothesis: When errors are decomposed with a consistent matched protocol (each GT and prediction assigned to exactly one error category), major architecture families exhibit signature error profiles (e.g., one family trades duplicates for misses, another trades localization for classification); most pairwise AP gaps are dominated by a single category, so category-targeted fixes could equalize families at far lower cost than adopting new architectures.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing errors for several checkpoint families on one dataset will show, for most pairs, one error category explaining the majority of the AP gap; simulated repair of that single category (oracle substitution) will close most of the gap.
why_important: Changes how architecture results are read and enables cheap targeted interventions instead of wholesale migrations.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: error-analysis toolkits exist; the claim of family-specific single-category dominance with oracle-repair quantification appears untested at systematic scale.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a consistent decomposition over 5-6 public checkpoints from 3 families; compute per-pair category contributions to AP gaps; run oracle-repair simulations per category.
main_risk: Decomposition protocols embed assignment choices that can shift category attribution; results must be shown stable across two protocols.
community_default_belief: Higher-AP architectures are better across the board; the gap reflects accumulated general superiority.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Architectural inductive biases are specific (set prediction vs dense scoring), so their consequences should be specific too; aggregate metrics just launder specificity into a scalar.
fastest_falsification: Fully post-hoc analysis over existing prediction files with an open-source decomposition protocol.

one_line: A cut-paste out-of-context evaluation isolates context reliance as a stable per-architecture scalar that standard AP conflates with recognition ability.
problem: Standard test sets preserve natural object-context correlations, so AP cannot distinguish recognizing objects from recognizing their habitual scenes.
core_hypothesis: Evaluating detectors on a controlled companion set where objects are composited into unfamiliar-but-plausible contexts yields a context-reliance score (in-context AP minus out-of-context AP, artifact-controlled); this score varies widely across architectures at matched standard AP and predicts robustness to natural distribution shifts better than standard AP does.
falsifiable_prediction: Checkpoints with matched standard AP will spread substantially on the context-reliance score; the score will correlate with performance drops on natural-shift evaluations more strongly than standard AP does.
why_important: Adds a second axis to detector evaluation that predicts real-world brittleness, cheap to produce from existing assets.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: out-of-context studies exist for classification and in small detection probes; a standardized reliance scalar validated as a shift-robustness predictor appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build the companion set via segmentation-based pasting with artifact controls (matched blending for in-context repastes); evaluate a checkpoint pool; correlate reliance scores with natural-shift performance drops.
main_risk: Pasting artifacts may dominate the measured drop; the in-context repaste control is essential and must be validated.
community_default_belief: Standard AP on held-out natural images adequately captures detection ability; context effects are second-order.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Held-out natural images share the training set's context statistics, so context shortcuts are rewarded identically at train and test - the metric is structurally blind to them.
fastest_falsification: A small pilot companion set (a few hundred composites) and two checkpoints suffice to see whether reliance scores spread at matched AP.

one_line: Categorical size buckets (small/medium/large) create boundary artifacts; continuous size-AP curves reveal crossovers that bucket metrics hide.
problem: Size-stratified AP uses fixed area thresholds, quantizing a continuous variable and inviting silent optimization toward bucket boundaries.
core_hypothesis: Model comparisons using bucketed size metrics mask crossover structure: one model can dominate another everywhere except a narrow size band (or vice versa) with identical bucket summaries; continuous AP-versus-size curves (kernel-smoothed matched-recall/precision) expose such crossovers, and for some checkpoint pairs the bucket verdict and the continuous-curve verdict disagree in practically relevant size ranges.
falsifiable_prediction: For a pool of checkpoint pairs, a measurable fraction will show size ranges where the bucket-level 'winner' is actually worse on the continuous curve, including ranges wider than a quarter octave of object size.
why_important: Applications care about specific size ranges (e.g., distant pedestrians); bucket summaries can recommend the wrong model for a given range.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: continuous stratification is occasionally plotted ad hoc; its systematic disagreement rate with bucket metrics appears unquantified.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute continuous size-performance curves with bootstrap bands for several checkpoints; count and characterize bucket-vs-curve verdict disagreements.
main_risk: Smoothing bandwidth choices affect curve details; conclusions must be shown bandwidth-stable.
community_default_belief: Three size buckets summarize scale behavior sufficiently for model comparison.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Detector scale behavior is shaped by discrete stride/pyramid structure, generating oscillatory or crossing patterns exactly the kind a three-bin summary integrates away.
fastest_falsification: Post-hoc curve computation over existing prediction files; disagreement counting is automatic.

one_line: Resolution-mismatch sensitivity is a stable, rankable model property that standard fixed-resolution evaluation never measures.
problem: Models are evaluated at their training-native resolution, but deployments run at whatever resolution latency budgets allow; sensitivity to that mismatch is uncharacterized and unreported.
core_hypothesis: Detectors differ systematically and stably in how gracefully AP degrades as inference resolution departs from training resolution (a 'resolution robustness' curve shaped by architecture and augmentation, consistent across datasets); two models with equal native-resolution AP can differ dramatically off-resolution, and the robustness curve rank is preserved across datasets, making it a legitimate reportable model property.
falsifiable_prediction: Measuring AP-versus-inference-resolution curves for a checkpoint pool on two datasets will show (a) large off-resolution spread among native-AP-matched models and (b) strong cross-dataset rank correlation of robustness scores.
why_important: Deployment reality is resolution-diverse; a standardized robustness curve would change model selection for edge and video applications.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: multi-resolution evaluation appears in passing; framing off-resolution robustness as a stable, cross-dataset-consistent model property with reporting standards appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate several public checkpoints across a resolution sweep on two datasets; quantify off-resolution spread at matched native AP and cross-dataset rank stability.
main_risk: Preprocessing details (resize algorithm, padding) may dominate the measured differences, requiring strict protocol standardization.
community_default_belief: Evaluating at the recommended resolution characterizes the model; off-resolution behavior is out-of-spec usage not worth measuring.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Off-spec usage is the norm in deployment, and the sensitivity varies enough across designs to flip real-world model choices.
fastest_falsification: A resolution sweep over existing checkpoints on one dataset already reveals whether native-AP-matched models spread off-resolution.

one_line: Score-free ranking metrics (recall versus detections-per-image curves) are more seed- and domain-stable than AP, making them better low-budget model selectors.
problem: Model selection under compute constraints uses noisy small-validation AP, which is sensitive to score calibration quirks that have nothing to do with detection competence.
core_hypothesis: Metrics that depend only on the ranking of detections (e.g., recall at k detections per image, area under recall-vs-budget curves) strip away score-scale artifacts and are therefore more stable across random seeds and more predictive of large-set AP and cross-domain AP than small-sample AP itself is.
falsifiable_prediction: On small validation samples, rank-based metrics will show lower cross-seed variance than AP and higher correlation with full-test-set AP; for cross-domain prediction, rank-based validation metrics will predict target-domain ordering better than source AP.
why_important: Cheaper, more reliable model selection benefits every practitioner running hyperparameter searches with limited evaluation budgets.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: ranking metrics exist in proposal evaluation; their systematic superiority as low-budget selection signals for full detectors appears unestablished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For a pool of checkpoints and multiple small validation subsamples, compute AP and rank-based metrics; compare variance and correlation with full-set AP; repeat across a domain pair.
main_risk: Rank-based metrics ignore calibration entirely, so they may mis-select when deployment requires thresholded operation at a fixed score.
community_default_belief: AP on a validation split is the gold-standard selection signal at any evaluation budget.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Small-sample AP inherits noise from score-tail interpolation and per-class averaging; rank metrics aggregate over exactly the stable part of model behavior.
fastest_falsification: Subsampling experiments over existing prediction files quantify the variance comparison without any training.

one_line: Detectors compress background rejection into a small set of feature-space prototypes whose drift predicts false-positive spikes under domain shift, label-free.
problem: FP rates explode unpredictably in new domains, and there is no label-free early-warning signal tied to a mechanism.
core_hypothesis: Negative decisions in a trained detector are mediated by a compact set of background prototypes (clusters in feature space covering most rejected locations); when a new domain's background features fall outside prototype coverage, rejection fails; therefore a coverage statistic computed on unlabeled target images predicts the FP increase before any labels exist.
falsifiable_prediction: Clustering rejected-location features on source data will yield few clusters covering most negatives; target-domain FP rates across several shifted datasets will correlate strongly with the measured prototype-coverage deficit on unlabeled target data.
why_important: A mechanistic, label-free FP forecaster enables deployment risk assessment and targeted background data collection.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: feature-space monitoring exists generically; grounding it in a background-prototype account of detection rejection with FP-specific prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Extract features at rejected locations on source validation data; cluster and measure coverage compactness; compute coverage deficits on unlabeled shifted datasets; correlate with realized FP rates measured using their labels.
main_risk: Foreground-adjacent negatives (hard negatives) may not be prototype-governed, breaking the coverage-FP link where it matters most.
community_default_belief: Background rejection is a diffuse property of the whole network, not localizable structure; FP prediction requires labeled target data.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Backgrounds are highly clustered in natural images (sky, road, vegetation, indoor surfaces); efficient networks plausibly exploit that clustering, creating exactly the compact structure claimed.
fastest_falsification: The clustering-compactness check on one checkpoint is a small inference-plus-analysis job; absence of compact structure kills the idea early.

one_line: Classes split bimodally into context-dependent and appearance-dependent groups, and the split predicts which classes cut-paste augmentation helps versus harms.
problem: Cut-paste augmentation produces inconsistent per-class results, and there is no predictive account of which classes benefit.
core_hypothesis: Per-class context reliance (measured by in-context vs out-of-context detection gap) is bimodal rather than continuous: classes are either context-anchored (small, ambiguous, habitual-location objects) or appearance-anchored; cut-paste augmentation improves appearance-anchored classes' robustness but actively degrades context-anchored classes' accuracy by destroying their primary evidence channel, making the reliance measurement a pre-training predictor of per-class augmentation outcome.
falsifiable_prediction: The distribution of per-class context-reliance scores will show two modes; per-class AP changes under cut-paste training will correlate strongly and negatively with pre-measured context reliance, with sign flips concentrated at the mode boundary.
why_important: Turns a hit-or-miss augmentation into a targeted tool applied per class, and establishes context reliance as a measurable class taxonomy.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: context effects and cut-paste are separately studied; using measured reliance to predict per-class augmentation outcomes appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-class reliance on an existing checkpoint via paste-based probes; train with class-uniform cut-paste; test the correlation between reliance and per-class AP change.
main_risk: Bimodality may be an artifact of class-size confounds (small objects are both context-reliant and paste-artifact-sensitive).
community_default_belief: Cut-paste is a broadly beneficial diversity augmentation whose per-class variance is random noise.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If context is some classes' main evidence, randomizing context is targeted evidence destruction for them - systematic, not noise.
fastest_falsification: The reliance measurement plus one cut-paste training run yields the correlation directly.

one_line: Co-occurrence priors live in the classification head, not the features: head transplantation moves context bias between detectors.
problem: Where detectors store contextual priors (features vs decision layers) is unknown, so debiasing efforts target the whole network blindly.
core_hypothesis: Object co-occurrence and scene-prior effects are implemented predominantly in the classification head's weighting of context-carrying feature channels, while backbone/neck features remain relatively context-neutral; transplanting the head from a context-biased model onto a context-neutral model's features (with light adapter alignment) transfers the measured context bias, and vice versa, localizing the bias to the head.
falsifiable_prediction: Head-swap composites will inherit the head donor's context-reliance score rather than the feature donor's, on paste-based context probes, across two architecture families.
why_important: If bias is head-localized, debiasing becomes a cheap head-retraining problem rather than full-model retraining, enabling context-adjustable detectors.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: representation-vs-head decompositions exist for classification fairness; the analogous localization of contextual priors in detection appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train context-biased and context-neutralized (cut-paste) variants sharing initialization; measure context reliance of the four head-feature combinations with paste probes.
main_risk: Head-feature co-adaptation may make transplants degenerate, requiring adapters that themselves confound the attribution.
community_default_belief: Contextual priors are woven through the entire feature hierarchy and cannot be surgically localized or moved.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Features are trained mainly by localization-driven gradients shared across classes, while class-conditional context weighting has nowhere to live but the head's class-specific parameters.
fastest_falsification: A two-model, four-combination probe study at small scale settles the localization question.

one_line: Negative context (scene-based implausibility) contributes more to detector precision than positive context contributes to recall - an exploitable asymmetry.
problem: Context effects are discussed monolithically, without separating the suppression of implausible detections from the boosting of plausible ones.
core_hypothesis: Detectors use scene evidence asymmetrically: suppression of contextually implausible candidates (negative context) is a stronger, more reliable effect than enhancement of contextually plausible ones (positive context); intervention studies (inserting objects into implausible scenes vs removing supportive context around plausible ones) will quantify a suppression-dominance ratio above one, implying that context-debiasing for open-world recall should target the suppression pathway specifically.
falsifiable_prediction: Score drops for objects pasted into implausible scenes will exceed score drops from neutralizing context around in-place objects, at matched paste quality; the asymmetry will hold across most classes and two architectures.
why_important: Open-world and rare-event detection fail exactly on implausible-context objects; knowing suppression dominates tells us what to fix and what to preserve.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: context studies measure aggregate effects; the suppression-vs-enhancement decomposition with matched interventions appears new for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build matched paste interventions (implausible insertion vs context neutralization) with blending controls; measure score deltas per class on existing checkpoints; compute the dominance ratio.
main_risk: Matching intervention strength between insertion and neutralization is nontrivial; unmatched interventions bias the ratio.
community_default_belief: Context helps detection symmetrically: plausible contexts boost and implausible contexts suppress, in comparable measure.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Training never shows objects in implausible contexts, so suppression generalizes unchecked, while positive context competes with strong appearance evidence and saturates.
fastest_falsification: Paste-based intervention studies are inference-only on existing checkpoints.

one_line: Part-whole false positives (detecting a wheel as a car, a face as a person) are removable by a training-free containment-consistency test.
problem: A persistent FP class consists of object parts detected as whole objects (or vice versa), and generic score thresholding cannot remove them without losing true detections.
core_hypothesis: Part-whole FPs have a structural signature: the false 'whole' detection is spatially contained in (or contains) a higher-evidence detection of the related category, with characteristic size ratios; a post-hoc consistency test over the detection set (checking containment relations against a small learned or hand-specified part-whole relation table) removes a large fraction of these FPs at negligible true-positive cost, without retraining.
falsifiable_prediction: Auditing FPs on existing checkpoints will show part-whole confusions forming a stable, identifiable percentage of high-confidence FPs; the containment filter will remove most of them while affecting under a small fraction of true positives.
why_important: A cheap, interpretable FP reducer targeting a failure family that annoys every practitioner and pollutes downstream counting.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: relational post-processing has appeared in older pipelines; a quantified modern audit plus a minimal containment rule evaluated on strong detectors appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Categorize top-confidence FPs on two checkpoints; measure part-whole share; implement the containment test with a small relation table; evaluate FP removal vs TP cost.
main_risk: Genuine nested objects (person in car, picture of an object) create true containment cases that the filter could wrongly suppress.
community_default_belief: Modern detectors' context modeling already resolves part-whole relations; remaining FPs are unstructured residue needing better features.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Per-box independent scoring has no mechanism to enforce inter-detection consistency; the information exists in the detection set but is never jointly consumed.
fastest_falsification: The FP audit alone (a few hours of categorization on existing outputs) establishes whether the failure family is big enough to matter.

one_line: Physical-artifact false positives (shadows, reflections, prints) share a single cross-class feature-space direction, enabling one-vector debiasing.
problem: Shadows, reflections, and printed pictures of objects trigger detections across many classes, and per-class fixes do not scale.
core_hypothesis: The features of artifact-triggered detections differ from real-object detections along a low-dimensional, class-shared direction (encoding cues like missing 3D shading structure, boundary inconsistency, or surface context); a single linear direction fitted on artifact examples from a few classes will separate artifact FPs in unseen classes too, and projecting it out (or thresholding along it) reduces artifact FPs broadly at minor TP cost.
falsifiable_prediction: A linear probe trained to separate artifact FPs from TPs on a subset of classes will transfer with high AUROC to held-out classes; feature-space edits along the fitted direction will reduce artifact FP rates across classes without retraining.
why_important: Artifact FPs are safety-relevant (braking for shadows, counting reflections) and a class-shared fix would be a rare cheap win.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: concept directions are studied in interpretability; an artifact-FP direction with cross-class transfer and an inference-time edit in detection appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect artifact FP examples (shadow/reflection/print) via targeted mining on existing checkpoints; fit the direction on half the classes; test separation transfer and the projection intervention on the rest.
main_risk: Artifact types may each need their own direction (shadows differ from prints), fragmenting the single-vector claim into a small subspace claim.
community_default_belief: Artifact robustness requires targeted training data (hard negatives of shadows/reflections) per deployment domain.
why_that_may_be_wrong: All these artifacts share the property of 2D appearance without consistent 3D object evidence, a cue plausibly encoded once in feature space rather than per class.
fastest_falsification: Direction fitting and held-out-class transfer testing are post-hoc on existing checkpoints and mined examples.

one_line: Detectors carry a learned per-image object-count prior that suppresses detections in dense scenes and inflates them in sparse ones.
problem: Recall in very dense scenes and precision in very sparse scenes are both anomalously bad, usually blamed on NMS or appearance, without considering a global count prior.
core_hypothesis: Training distributions concentrate object counts in a moderate range; detectors internalize this as a soft prior on total detections per image (via global feature pathways and score normalization effects), so per-image predicted counts regress toward the training mode: dense scenes are under-counted beyond what per-object difficulty explains, and near-empty scenes over-counted; conditioning score calibration on estimated scene density counteracts the prior and improves both tails.
falsifiable_prediction: Predicted-vs-true count curves will show systematic regression toward the training-count mode after controlling for per-object difficulty (occlusion, size); density-conditioned recalibration will improve dense-scene recall and sparse-scene precision simultaneously.
why_important: Count-critical applications (retail shelves, crowds, wildlife surveys) live in the distribution tails where this prior does the most damage.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: density estimation literature knows count biases; attributing tail failures of standard detectors to an internalized count prior with a conditioning fix appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Bin validation images by GT count; fit predicted-count curves controlling for difficulty covariates; test the regression-to-mode signature; apply density-conditioned calibration and re-measure tail performance.
main_risk: Difficulty covariates may not fully capture why dense scenes are harder, leaving residual confounding of the prior signature.
community_default_belief: Detectors score each candidate location independently; scene-level count priors have no pathway into per-box decisions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Global pooling, normalization layers, and attention give every box a scene-level pathway; nothing prevents count statistics from leaking into it during training.
fastest_falsification: The regression-to-mode analysis is post-hoc on existing predictions with GT counts.

one_line: Learned camera-geometry priors cause position-conditional misses (elevated cars, low-flying objects), and position-shuffled training trades measured in-position AP for out-of-position robustness.
problem: Detectors fail on objects in geometrically unusual image positions, a safety-relevant blind spot invisible in standard evaluation because test sets share the training position statistics.
core_hypothesis: Detectors internalize scene geometry regularities (cars on the ground plane band, lights near the top), making detection probability depend on image position beyond appearance; the strength of the positional prior is measurable by paste interventions at controlled positions, and position-randomized augmentation reduces the positional dependence at a quantifiable cost to in-distribution AP - a tunable tradeoff, not a free fix.
falsifiable_prediction: Score-vs-position maps for pasted objects will show strong class-specific positional structure matching training statistics; position-shuffled training will flatten the maps while reducing standard AP by a measurable, schedule-dependent amount.
why_important: Quantifies a safety blind spot (unusual viewpoints, banked roads, aerial anomalies) and characterizes the robustness-accuracy exchange rate for fixing it.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: position bias is known in classification saliency; a quantitative positional-prior map for detection with an explicit tradeoff characterization appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Paste class instances across a grid of positions on neutral scenes; map score vs position for existing checkpoints; train a position-shuffled variant; compare maps and standard AP.
main_risk: Paste realism varies with position (scale-position correlations in natural scenes), confounding the map unless scale is controlled.
community_default_belief: Convolutional and windowed architectures are translation-equivariant enough that image position plays no meaningful role in detection decisions.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Padding, positional encodings, multi-scale assignment, and biased training statistics all break equivariance in practice; the question is magnitude, which no one measures.
fastest_falsification: The paste-grid score map on one checkpoint is inference-only and immediately shows whether positional structure exists.

one_line: Inter-object score interference is asymmetric by size: adding a large object suppresses nearby small-object scores far more than the reverse.
problem: Detections are treated as independent given the image, but adding or removing one object changes others' scores in unquantified ways that matter for cluttered scenes.
core_hypothesis: Feature pooling, attention normalization, and suppression stages make each detection's score depend on other objects present, and the dependence is size-asymmetric: large objects capture shared feature capacity and attention mass, measurably suppressing nearby small-object scores, while small objects barely affect large ones; the interference decays with distance on a characteristic length scale that differs by architecture family.
falsifiable_prediction: Controlled paste/removal interventions will show score changes on neighbors with a large-to-small effect several times the small-to-large effect, and interference-vs-distance curves will fit an architecture-specific decay length stable across scenes.
why_important: Explains why small objects vanish next to big ones in practice, and yields an interference length as a new architecture-comparison property relevant to cluttered-scene applications.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: contextual interactions are studied semantically; a quantitative, size-asymmetric interference law with measured decay lengths appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Using segmentation-based object removal/insertion with inpainting controls, measure neighbor score deltas as functions of size pair and distance on two checkpoints; fit asymmetry ratios and decay lengths.
main_risk: Inpainting artifacts may themselves perturb scores; artifact-only controls (inpaint without object change) are mandatory.
community_default_belief: Given the pixels, detections are effectively independent; inter-object effects are second-order curiosities.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Shared normalization and attention are zero-sum mechanisms: mass allocated to one region is taken from another, predicting first-order interference the independence assumption ignores.
fastest_falsification: A small intervention set (dozens of scenes) on one checkpoint reveals whether the asymmetry ratio is large.

one_line: Background texture entropy predicts per-image false-positive count better than object count or image size, enabling entropy-adaptive thresholds.
problem: Per-image FP burden varies wildly, and fixed thresholds overshoot on busy images while wasting recall on clean ones; no cheap image-level FP predictor is established.
core_hypothesis: FP generation is driven primarily by background texture complexity (entropy/edge density of non-object regions offering more spurious pattern matches), not by scene object count or resolution; a cheap texture-entropy statistic predicts per-image FP counts well, and an entropy-conditioned score threshold improves image-level precision at fixed aggregate recall over any global threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: Across validation images, texture entropy will out-predict object count and image size for FP count (higher explained variance); the entropy-adaptive threshold will Pareto-dominate fixed thresholds on the precision-recall-per-image frontier.
why_important: A zero-training deployment knob that reallocates the FP budget by image difficulty, valuable for review pipelines and alerting systems.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: image-difficulty prediction exists broadly; the specific dominance of background entropy for FP prediction and its use as a threshold conditioner appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute texture statistics on validation images; regress per-image FP counts on entropy, object count, and size; implement the adaptive threshold and evaluate the per-image precision-recall frontier.
main_risk: Entropy correlates with scene type (urban vs nature), so the predictor may be a scene-type proxy that fails within scene types.
community_default_belief: FPs are model- and object-driven; image-level covariates are too crude to be operationally useful.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Spurious pattern matches are a stochastic function of how much pattern the background offers - a first-order textural quantity, not a subtle model property.
fastest_falsification: The regression study is pure post-processing over existing predictions and images.

one_line: Test-time augmentation benefit is predictable per model from a training-augmentation saturation score: TTA is redundant augmentation.
problem: TTA doubles or quadruples inference cost, and whether a given model will benefit is discovered only by trying it.
core_hypothesis: TTA (flips, multi-scale) helps exactly to the degree that the model failed to internalize the corresponding invariance during training; a cheap 'augmentation saturation' score (agreement between the model's outputs on augmented input pairs, measured on unlabeled data) therefore predicts each model's TTA gain, with strongly augmented modern recipes near saturation (TTA wasted) and lightly augmented models below it (TTA valuable).
falsifiable_prediction: Across a pool of checkpoints with diverse training recipes, TTA gain will correlate strongly and negatively with the saturation score; a decision rule from the score will predict which models gain non-trivially from TTA with high accuracy, using no labels.
why_important: Converts an expensive trial-and-error deployment decision into a cheap unlabeled measurement, saving inference cost fleet-wide.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: TTA and augmentation are both mature topics, but a quantitative redundancy law connecting training-augmentation saturation to TTA benefit in detection appears unformulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For several public checkpoints, compute flip/scale agreement scores on unlabeled images; measure actual TTA AP gains; test the correlation and the decision rule on held-out models.
main_risk: TTA gains also flow from ensembling noise reduction unrelated to invariance, adding an offset the saturation score cannot see.
community_default_belief: TTA is a generic accuracy knob worth trying on any model when inference budget allows.
why_that_may_be_wrong: If invariance is already learned, augmented views are near-duplicates and averaging them cannot add information; the benefit must come from the invariance gap, which is measurable in advance.
fastest_falsification: Agreement scores and TTA evaluation on a handful of checkpoints suffice for a first correlation estimate; all inference-only.

one_line: Video detection flicker is mostly score oscillation around the threshold, not feature instability; temporal score smoothing alone removes most of it.
problem: Frame-to-frame detection flicker plagues video deployment and motivates heavy temporal architectures, without a decomposition of what actually flickers.
core_hypothesis: For static or slowly moving objects, the underlying localization and features are frame-stable; flicker arises because scores hover near the operating threshold and cross it with per-frame noise; consequently exponential smoothing of matched detection scores across frames (no feature-level temporal modeling, no tracking beyond greedy IoU matching) eliminates the majority of identity flicker at negligible compute, bounding the value of temporal feature architectures for this specific failure mode.
falsifiable_prediction: Decomposing flicker events on video datasets will attribute most to near-threshold score crossings with stable boxes; score-smoothing will reduce flicker metrics by a large fraction while leaving AP essentially unchanged, across two single-frame detectors.
why_important: Correct attribution prevents over-engineering: if a filter fixes flicker, temporal architectures must justify themselves on other failure modes (occlusion, motion blur).
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: temporal smoothing is folk practice; a quantified flicker decomposition establishing score-crossing dominance and bounding architectural headroom appears unpublished to my knowledge.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run single-frame detectors on video data with GT; classify flicker events (score-crossing vs box-jump vs class-switch); apply score smoothing; measure flicker reduction and AP impact.
main_risk: Flicker composition may differ sharply by domain (dashcam vs surveillance), limiting the universality of the dominance claim.
community_default_belief: Flicker reflects unstable per-frame perception and requires temporal feature aggregation or tracking-based stabilization to fix.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Thresholding converts tiny continuous fluctuations into binary flicker; the visible instability may be an artifact of the decision rule rather than perception.
fastest_falsification: The flicker-event classification on one video dataset with one detector is a small inference-plus-analysis job.

one_line: Quantization degrades localization before classification: box quality collapses at bit-widths where class accuracy still holds, motivating branch-asymmetric precision.
problem: Detector quantization is tuned against aggregate AP, hiding which sub-task fails first as precision drops, so mixed-precision budgets are allocated blindly.
core_hypothesis: Box regression outputs are continuous and sensitive to activation resolution, while classification decisions have wide margins; therefore, as weights/activations are quantized more aggressively, localization error (AP75, matched IoU) degrades earlier and faster than classification accuracy, and allocating higher precision only to the regression pathway (head and last neck stage) recovers most full-precision AP at nearly the low-precision compute cost.
falsifiable_prediction: A bit-width sweep will show AP75 dropping at a higher bit-width than classification-only metrics; branch-asymmetric quantization will dominate uniform quantization on the AP-vs-compute frontier across two architectures.
why_important: Edge deployment of detectors is bottlenecked by quantization losses; knowing the failure order turns mixed-precision design from search into principle.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: mixed-precision detection exists via automated search; the specific ordered-degradation law and its use as a design shortcut appear unarticulated.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Post-training-quantize a detector at several bit-widths; measure classification-only and localization-only degradation curves; implement regression-branch-only high precision and compare frontiers.
main_risk: Quantization-aware training may equalize the degradation order, restricting the claim to post-training quantization regimes.
community_default_belief: Quantization sensitivity is layer-depth and layer-type driven; sub-task asymmetry is not a primary organizing principle.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Task output geometry (continuous regression vs margin-protected classification) is a fundamental sensitivity difference that layer-centric analyses average away.
fastest_falsification: Post-training quantization sweeps with task-decomposed metrics require no training and modest engineering.

one_line: A small identifiable subset of normalization layers causes batch-size-1 inference score shifts, with object-size-dependent effects fixable by targeted statistic freezing.
problem: Detectors trained with batch statistics behave differently at deployment batch size 1, and the shift is treated as a diffuse nuisance handled by global BN freezing or sync tricks.
core_hypothesis: The train-to-deployment statistic mismatch is concentrated: a small subset of normalization layers (those whose activation statistics vary most with scene composition) accounts for most of the score shift, and the shift is object-size-dependent (small-object scores move most because their evidence is normalization-sensitive); freezing or recalibrating only the culprit layers removes most of the shift, preserving whatever adaptivity the rest provide.
falsifiable_prediction: Layer-wise interventions will reveal a minority of layers explaining the majority of batch-size-induced score shift; the shift magnitude will decrease with object size; targeted freezing will match or beat global freezing on deployment-condition AP.
why_important: Batch-condition mismatch quietly costs accuracy in nearly every deployment; a surgical fix beats blunt global freezing.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: BN train-test mismatch is known generally; the concentration claim, size-dependence, and targeted-freeze remedy for detection appear unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare per-detection scores under training-style batches vs batch-1 inference; attribute shifts layer-wise by swapping statistics one layer at a time; test size dependence; evaluate targeted vs global freezing.
main_risk: Layer interactions may make one-at-a-time attribution misleading, requiring costlier group interventions.
community_default_belief: Freezing all normalization statistics at deployment is the correct and complete fix; finer structure is not worth investigating.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Global freezing throws away beneficial adaptivity along with the harmful variance; if the harm is concentrated, the blunt fix is leaving accuracy on the table.
fastest_falsification: Layer-swap attribution is inference-only with statistic bookkeeping on one checkpoint.

one_line: Background texture insertions suppress detections within a measurable spatial radius, defining an architecture-specific interference range that predicts clutter robustness.
problem: Detectors fail near cluttered or textured regions in ways described only anecdotally; there is no standard measurement of how far background content reaches into detection decisions.
core_hypothesis: Inserting high-saliency distractor texture at a controlled distance from a target object suppresses the target's score by an amount that decays with distance according to an architecture-characteristic interference profile (set by receptive fields, attention patterns, and normalization); this measured interference radius is a stable model property that predicts relative performance degradation on naturally cluttered scenes better than standard AP does.
falsifiable_prediction: Distance-sweep insertion experiments will yield smooth, reproducible suppression-vs-distance profiles differing across architecture families; profile-derived interference radii will rank models on natural clutter-heavy subsets more accurately than their standard AP ranks.
why_important: Gives a laboratory-style probe for a deployment-critical property (clutter tolerance), usable for model selection without collecting cluttered test data.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: adversarial patches show existence of remote interference; a calibrated interference-radius measurement as a benign, predictive model property appears undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct distance-sweep texture insertions around fixed target objects; measure suppression profiles for several checkpoints; correlate radii with performance on naturally cluttered evaluation subsets.
main_risk: Suppression may depend more on texture content than distance, making a single radius an oversimplification.
community_default_belief: Clutter robustness is an emergent property visible only in end-to-end evaluation on cluttered data; it cannot be probed synthetically.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Interference is mediated by concrete architectural mechanisms with characteristic spatial scales; those scales are exactly what controlled probes measure best.
fastest_falsification: Insertion sweeps on one checkpoint establish whether profiles are smooth and stable; all inference-only.

one_line: Recall degrades in discrete stair-steps as inference resolution drops, aligned with stride-boundary crossings of object pixel sizes, so deployment resolutions should snap to critical points.
problem: Resolution is treated as a smooth accuracy-latency dial, but architectures process objects in stride-quantized regimes that may make the dial discontinuous.
core_hypothesis: As input resolution decreases, cohorts of objects cross assignment/pyramid-level boundaries together (their pixel sizes fall below per-level minima), producing stair-step drops in recall at predictable resolutions determined by the object-size distribution and the model's stride/level configuration; between steps, resolution reductions are nearly free, so latency tuning should jump between step edges rather than sample the dial uniformly.
falsifiable_prediction: Fine-grained resolution sweeps will show recall-vs-resolution curves with statistically significant step structure at resolutions predicted from stride arithmetic and the dataset size histogram, consistent across models sharing stride configuration and absent in stride-configurations predicting different step locations.
why_important: Deployment teams choose resolutions constantly; knowing the safe plateaus and cliff edges converts guesswork into arithmetic.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: resolution-accuracy tradeoffs are benchmarked coarsely; the stride-predicted step structure and its use for operating-point selection appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sweep inference resolution at fine granularity for two checkpoints with different stride configurations; test for step structure at the predicted locations; verify plateau flatness between steps.
main_risk: Size-distribution smoothness in natural datasets may blur the steps below detectability, even if the mechanism is real per object.
community_default_belief: Accuracy varies smoothly with resolution; any nearby resolution is an equivalent operating point at proportional cost.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Multi-scale detectors have hard per-level object-size ranges; whole object cohorts change processing regime simultaneously at specific scales, which is a step-generating mechanism.
fastest_falsification: A fine resolution sweep on one checkpoint (inference-only) either shows the predicted steps or does not.

one_line: Motion-blur 'detection failure' is substantially a localization-convention mismatch: models find blurred objects but place boxes at the blur centroid while annotations follow sharp-frame conventions.
problem: Benchmarks report large detection drops under motion blur, interpreted as recognition failure, guiding robustness research toward feature invariance.
core_hypothesis: Under motion blur, a meaningful fraction of measured failure is not missed recognition but box-placement disagreement: the physically ambiguous extent of a blurred object (leading edge vs trailing edge vs centroid) is resolved differently by models and by annotation conventions, so IoU-based matching fails despite successful detection; evaluating with blur-aware matching (relaxed or convention-normalized along the motion axis) recovers a substantial fraction of the apparent robustness gap.
falsifiable_prediction: Analyzing blur-failure cases will show a large share with confident detections displaced along the motion axis; motion-axis-relaxed evaluation will recover a significant portion of the AP drop, while non-blurred evaluation is unaffected by the relaxation.
why_important: Misdiagnosed failure modes misdirect research; if evaluation convention explains much of the blur gap, the fix is metrics and label conventions, not new architectures.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: blur robustness is benchmarked routinely; the convention-mismatch decomposition of the blur gap appears unperformed.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Apply controlled synthetic motion blur to labeled images; categorize failures (miss vs axis-displaced box); evaluate with and without motion-axis-relaxed matching; quantify recovered AP.
main_risk: Synthetic blur may not reproduce natural blur's annotation ambiguity; a small real-blur validation set is needed.
community_default_belief: Motion blur destroys the features detectors rely on; the AP drop measures genuine perceptual failure requiring robust training.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Blur does not delete objects, it smears their extent; extent ambiguity is a labeling problem first, and IoU matching converts label ambiguity into fake misses.
fastest_falsification: The failure-categorization on synthetically blurred data with an existing checkpoint is a quick inference study.

one_line: Per-image difficulty-based resolution routing beats any fixed-resolution configuration on the AP-per-FLOP frontier, and difficulty is predictable from cheap image features.
problem: Deployment picks one resolution for all images, but most images are easy at low resolution and only some need expensive high-resolution processing.
core_hypothesis: Per-image detection difficulty (whether high resolution changes the outcome) is predictable from cheap covariates (thumbnail-based small-object likelihood, edge density, a tiny proxy model's confidence profile); routing only predicted-hard images to high resolution achieves a strictly better AP-versus-compute frontier than every fixed resolution, with the routing predictor requiring orders of magnitude less compute than the savings it enables.
falsifiable_prediction: An oracle router (choosing per-image resolution by actual outcome difference) will show a large frontier improvement, establishing headroom; a cheap learned router will capture a substantial fraction of the oracle gain on held-out data.
why_important: Inference cost dominates detection economics at fleet scale; input-adaptive routing is a directly deployable efficiency multiplier.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: adaptive computation exists inside networks; simple outside-the-model resolution routing for detection, with a quantified oracle-headroom analysis, appears underexplored relative to its simplicity.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate a checkpoint at two resolutions on validation data; compute oracle routing headroom; train a lightweight router on cheap features; measure captured fraction on held-out images.
main_risk: If per-image outcome differences are dominated by unpredictable borderline noise rather than stable image properties, the learned router will capture little of the oracle gain.
community_default_belief: Resolution is a global deployment constant; per-image adaptivity belongs inside exotic dynamic architectures, not deployment wrappers.
why_that_may_be_wrong: The difficulty signal (are there small objects?) is largely a property of the scene visible even at thumbnail scale, requiring no exotic machinery to read.
fastest_falsification: The oracle-headroom computation is pure re-analysis of two-resolution inference outputs; if headroom is small, the idea dies before any router is built.

one_line: Ensemble gains in detection are predictable from single-model score-gap statistics: disagreement lives on a stable ambiguity set visible to one model.
problem: Whether an ensemble is worth its cost is discovered only after training and running multiple models.
core_hypothesis: Detector ensemble improvements concentrate on a stable subset of objects characterized by intra-model ambiguity signals (small top-score margins, duplicate structure, unstable boxes under jitter); because these signals are measurable on one model, the achievable ensemble gain (and where it will land - which classes, sizes, scene types) is predictable before building the ensemble, within a useful tolerance.
falsifiable_prediction: Cross-model disagreement (measured on actual ensembles) will overlap heavily with the single-model ambiguity set; a predictor of ensemble AP gain fitted on some datasets/models will transfer to held-out models with small error, using single-model statistics only.
why_important: Lets teams decide between ensembling, more data, or bigger single models using one cheap measurement instead of expensive trial ensembles.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: ensemble diversity prediction exists in classification; a detection-specific formulation using detection-native ambiguity signals (duplicates, box jitter) appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train or gather several detector pools; measure per-object ensemble effects; compute single-model ambiguity statistics; test overlap and fit the gain predictor with held-out validation.
main_risk: Heterogeneous-architecture ensembles may derive gains from complementary biases invisible to any single member's ambiguity signals.
community_default_belief: Ensemble benefit reflects inter-model diversity that cannot be known from any single member.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Most disagreement between similarly trained models occurs where the task itself is ambiguous - a data property, not a model-pair property, and data properties are visible to one model.
fastest_falsification: If any two seeds of a public detector exist, the overlap between their disagreement set and one seed's ambiguity set is an immediate inference-only test.

one_line: In streaming detection, latency jitter (variance) degrades effective accuracy more than equal-mean latency increase: stability beats speed near real-time thresholds.
problem: Streaming perception optimizes mean latency, but real systems exhibit latency variance from contention and input-dependent compute, with unquantified accuracy consequences.
core_hypothesis: For dynamic scenes, the accuracy cost of a late result grows superlinearly with delay (objects move, matches expire), so a latency distribution's variance contributes disproportionately to streaming detection error: a configuration with slightly higher mean but low jitter (e.g., fixed compute paths, reserved resources) outperforms a faster-on-average but jittery configuration in streaming metrics, and the crossover is predictable from scene motion statistics.
falsifiable_prediction: Streaming evaluation with controlled synthetic latency distributions (same mean, different variances) will show accuracy decreasing with variance at fixed mean; a jitter-penalized scheduler will beat a mean-optimal scheduler on the same hardware trace, with the gap growing with scene motion speed.
why_important: Changes the optimization target for real-time perception systems from mean speed to latency distribution shaping - actionable in deployment engineering.
why_possibly_novel: Unverified: streaming-perception metrics account for delay, but isolating variance from mean as the dominant term with a scheduling consequence appears unexplored.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Replay video datasets through a streaming evaluation harness injecting latency distributions with matched means and varying variance; measure streaming AP; compare jitter-penalized vs mean-optimal configurations.
main_risk: The effect size depends heavily on motion statistics; slow-scene domains may show negligible variance sensitivity, narrowing applicability.
community_default_belief: Faster average inference is better for streaming perception; variance is an engineering nuisance orthogonal to accuracy.
why_that_may_be_wrong: Delay cost is convex in delay for moving scenes; by Jensen's inequality, variance strictly increases expected cost at fixed mean - the accuracy metric is variance-sensitive by construction.
fastest_falsification: The synthetic latency-injection study needs only an existing detector, video data, and a replay harness - no training.
